column53: The Coddington Twin Springs Ranch has been in our family since 1901 and was once an official post office when mail was delivered by horseback. Today, we manage the 640-acre property through sustainable grazing, mechanical and manual noxious weed control, and pasture restoration. We’ve invested in essential equipment and have successfully removed invasive species like bull thistle, musk thistle, and star thistle over several years. Our long-term commitment, consistent stewardship, and proactive community engagement demonstrate our proven capacity to implement and sustain effective land management practices.
column72: Comprehensive Thistle Management Initiative at The Coddington Twin Springs Ranch
column73: Education and Outreach Early Detection & Rapid Response (EDRR) Surveying and Mapping Integrated Weed Management (On-the-Ground Treatments) Planning, Capacity Development, and Partnership Building
column77: We seek support to manage invasive thistles impacting our grasslands through mechanical, chemical, and manual treatments, while also engaging neighboring landowners—many of whom are elderly or infirm—in outreach and education to promote long-term, community-based weed management.
column78: For several years, we have been actively working to combat the infestation of noxious thistles, which continue to impact the health and productivity of our grasslands, which reduce forage for livestock and native wildlife. Several varieties of thistles have been identified on the property, including bull thistles, musk thistles, and star thistles. We have been working to eradicate thistles from our grassland for numerous years, but additional resources are now required to manage this invasive species more effectively. The objective is to restore the ecological balance and productive capacity of the Coddington Twin Springs Ranch through a combination of mechanical, chemical, and manual thistle management methods. An integral part of this effort includes community outreach and education, especially for neighboring elderly and infirm landowners who are less able to manage thistle outbreaks on their own.

column97: This project is needed to control the rapid spread of invasive thistle species—specifically bull, musk, and star thistles—which are reducing native plant diversity and forage availability on our ranch. Without intervention, these weeds will continue to threaten the ecological health and productivity of our grasslands, as well as neighboring properties. Additional resources are essential to implement effective, large-scale treatments and engage surrounding landowners in coordinated management and prevention efforts.
column98: This project will improve forage availability for livestock and wildlife by restoring native grasslands, which supports local agricultural productivity and biodiversity. Reducing the spread of invasive thistles also decreases future treatment costs for neighboring landowners and protects the long-term health of shared rangelands.
column99: This project builds on years of manual thistle removal by adding herbicide use, GPS mapping, and community outreach to expand impact and efficiency.
column100: We will engage neighboring landowners—many of whom are elderly or infirm—as informal partners in this project. Through direct outreach and community workshops, we aim to increase awareness, share management strategies, and coordinate thistle removal efforts on adjacent properties. While we do not have formal agreements in place, our collaborative approach is rooted in mutual interest and long-standing relationships within the community. Additionally, we intend to utilize guidance from local agricultural extension resources when needed. These partnerships will enhance the project by expanding the treatment area beyond our own land, encouraging long-term weed management practices among neighbors, and promoting collective responsibility for preserving native grasslands. Supporting others who may not have the resources to act alone strengthens regional impact and reinforces the sustainability of our efforts. This cooperative model also fosters knowledge exchange and strengthens community resilience in managing invasive plant threats across private and public lands.

Host Community Workshop #1 to educate neighbors and introduce project goals

June – July 2025: 

Implement Integrated Weed Management through targeted herbicide application in high-density areas

Continue EDRR for any new thistle emergence

Begin mechanical and manual removal on accessible acreage

Conduct outreach to neighboring landowners using UTV

August 2025: 

Host Community Workshop #2 with updated mapping data and treatment strategies

Continue weed management treatments and monitoring

September – October 2025: 

Ongoing Surveying and Mapping to track treatment effectiveness

Maintain EDRR response and community support

Begin drafting long-term management and Planning & Capacity Development guide

November 2025: 

Final treatments and monitoring

Host Community Workshop #3 to share results and sustainability strategies

Submit final project report and maps
column103: Post-treatment monitoring will include repeated GPS-based mapping to compare thistle density before and after treatment. We will visually inspect treated areas monthly through November 2025 and track regrowth patterns to assess treatment effectiveness. Monitoring will continue annually during peak growth seasons, with manual removal of any regrowth as needed. All data collected will be documented and shared with neighbors during future outreach efforts to support regional weed management continuity.

column78:
Grazing is the act of animals, especially livestock like cattle, sheep, and goats, eating grass and other vegetation while roaming freely in a pasture or field.
Cabezon, located in a semi-arid region, has a history of livestock grazing, which is still practiced in many areas.
Noxious Weeds:
In the context of grazing, it's important to consider the presence of noxious weeds, which are plants designated by government entities as harmful to agriculture, wildlife, or property.
Invasive plant control methods, such as herbicides, are sometimes used to manage vegetation in grazing areas, according to DC.gov.
Some of the commonly used herbicides for invasive plant control include glyphosat (the active ingredient in Roundup™ and Rodeo™) and triclopyr (the active ingredient in Brush-BGone™ and Garlon™).

column97:
water is most precious resource and to help protect it is paramount to our survival.  These species are a direct hindrance to the protection of that resource. 
    
    Noxious weeds often displace native plants, leading to biodiversity loss. Controlling them allows native species to thrive, restoring natural ecosystems and their functions.
    Improved water quality:
    Some noxious weeds can contribute to decreased water quality. Their removal can improve water quality by preventing runoff and erosion.

    Noxious weeds can contribute to soil erosion, particularly on slopes and in areas with poor soil structure. Controlling them can help stabilize the soil and reduce erosion.
    Reduced fire risk:
    Certain noxious weeds can increase the risk of wildfires. Their removal can reduce fire hazards and protect communities and natural areas.
    Improved wildlife habitat:
    By restoring native vegetation, noxious weed control can improve wildlife habitat and support a wider variety of plant and animal species.
column98:
Reduced agricultural losses:
Noxious weeds can significantly reduce crop yields and forage availability for livestock, leading to economic losses for farmers and ranchers. Controlling these weeds can help restore productivity and reduce these losses. 
Lower herbicide costs:
While herbicide use can be a component of weed control, effective weed management strategies can reduce the overall need for herbicides, lowering costs associated with their purchase and application. 
Increased land productivity:
By removing noxious weeds, more land becomes available for productive activities, increasing the overall carrying capacity of farms and ranches. 
Improved infrastructure:
Noxious weeds can damage infrastructure like roads and buildings. Controlling them can reduce maintenance and repair costs

column77: This project aims to improve the mapping and the treatment efficiency of African rue. Our goals for the project are to collect data on infestations, adjust treatment timing, increase treatment efficiency, measure results, and share management resources with our partners.
column78: The goals of this project are to improve documentation of the extent of African rue infestations in southeastern New Mexico on private land, public land, and leased roadways, to efficiently and strategically treat infestations with our partners twice a year for multiple years to gain control, and increase our management strategies and success. By utilizing EDDMapS to report populations of African rue, infestation density and size, and showing other how to use this mapping program can improve our public awareness to the true extent of this noxious weed in our region. We plan to work with our partners to streamline herbicide treatments to hopefully prevent chemical resistance that has been witnessed at some sites. For this project, the Noxious Weed Coordinator of CSWCD will dedicate time to mapping infestations, checking 50 meters past infestations borders, taking polygons of large infestations, monitoring treatment sites, spot treatments where contractors will not be focused on, and make brochures on identifying African rue and using EDDMapS for noxious weeds reporting while in the field for our partners. Collectively, we will use Arsenal, a non-selective herbicide, at 2.5% to treat African rue twice a year during its growing seasons and before the flowers bloom in hopes of reducing the seed output by applying herbicide early enough to prevent successful development.

column97: The need for this project is to begin filling the massive data gap of the extent of African rue infestations and to improve our management tactics to prevent  unmanageable future infestations across southeastern New Mexico. Many ranchers and farmers know about this problematic weed, its resilience in extreme desert habitat, and its toxicity to livestock; however, it is so prevalent, and management efforts are having low success. By utilizing EDDMapS, dedicating time for mapping infestations, measuring population density and percent cover, adjusting herbicide application timing (before bloom rather than after bloom) and making educational materials available, we can better support our ranchers, farmers, wildlife stewards, and industry partners in our fight against African Rue in Southeastern New Mexico. Our partners make the efforts easier by granting us permission to treat and manage on land used for industry work where there is a constant influx of vehicles and materials.
column98: The residents of southeastern New Mexico will benefit from the African Rue Mapping and Management Project because of the economic and environmental investments that will come from adjusting and emphasize the importance of management and treatment protocols for African rue. Noxious weed management can offset the future costs of potential erosion problems, livestock loss, soil depletion from monoculture infestations and land productivity, that increase radically with unmanaged invasive species spreading unchecked. By having working relationships with industry partners, we can cover more land than with their cooperation and support. Our project also will benefit the residents by promoting the importance of noxious weed management through partnership outreach, education, and conservation of natural resources for the health and well-being of our district’s people and land for current and future generations.

column73: Integrated Weed Management (On-the-Ground Treatments)
column77: This project focuses on controlling noxious weeds on agricultural land using either mechanical or chemical treatments. By collaborating with producers, we aim to reduce weed populations, improve land productivity, and provide sustainable land management solutions.
column78:
This project focuses on managing and controlling noxious weeds on agricultural land to improve land health and productivity. In collaboration with producers, we will implement either mechanical or chemical treatment methods, depending on the specific needs of the land and the extent of the weed infestation. This approach allows for flexibility while ensuring that effective weed control strategies are applied.

The first phase of the project will involve detailed surveying and mapping of the land to assess the spread and density of noxious weeds. Based on this data, we will determine the most appropriate treatment method. Mechanical treatments, such as mowing, tilling, or cutting, will be used to physically remove weeds and limit their ability to spread. Alternatively, chemical treatments will be used in areas where mechanical methods are less effective, applying herbicides in a targeted manner to minimize environmental impact while controlling stubborn weed populations.

Throughout the project, ongoing monitoring will ensure that treatments are effective and that any necessary follow-up actions are identified. The final phase will involve an evaluation of treatment success, including a comprehensive report on the reduction of noxious weeds and the overall improvement of land conditions. This project will provide producers with the tools and knowledge to manage noxious weeds sustainably, ensuring healthier land and more productive agricultural operations in the future.

The SW Quay Soil and Water Conservation District (SWCD) is enthusiastic about collaborating with local producers to address the issue of unwanted and noxious weeds in our region. Our expansive landscape, characterized by numerous acres of stunning rangeland, presents a unique opportunity for improvement. Our goal is to enhance the quality of this land for our producers by implementing effective brush control practices aimed at eliminating invasive weed species.
Through these efforts, we aim to foster the growth of beneficial native grasses, which will not only bolster the health of our ecosystems but also support the productivity of agricultural operations in the area. By working together, we can create a sustainable and thriving environment that benefits both our land and the producers who depend on it. We look forward to engaging with our community to ensure the success of these vital conservation initiatives.
column98:
The project aimed at controlling unwanted and noxious weeds in the area offers significant economic and environmental benefits for local residents. Economically, enhancing the quality of rangeland will increase agricultural productivity by promoting the growth of native grasses, which improves forage quality for livestock. This can lead to higher farm yields and increased property values, as healthy land is more desirable to potential buyers. Additionally, reducing the need for herbicides can result in cost savings for producers.
Environmentally, the project fosters biodiversity by restoring native plant communities, which supports a diverse range of wildlife. Improved soil health from native grasses enhances soil structure and fertility, reducing erosion and promoting better water retention. Furthermore, healthier rangelands contribute to water quality protection by minimizing runoff and sedimentation in local water bodies. Overall, this initiative enhances agricultural viability while promoting environmental stewardship and sustainability for the entire community.

column77: Colfax SWCD proposes mapping and treatment of noxious thistle across 450 acres near Black Lake, NM. Rocky Mountain Ecology (RME) would implement project activities and has successfully teamed with both the NMSLO and CSWCD in the past.
column78:
The New Mexico State Land Office (NMSLO) has conducted targeted forest restoration and fuels reduction treatments in the Black Lake area since 2007.   Active forest management including forest thinning, prescribed fire, and removal of forest products have been essential to increasing the area’s ecosystem resilience to wildfire and reduce detrimental impacts of wildfire to the surrounding communities and watershed. Forest treatments have unfortunately propagated substantial populations of noxious weeds in the area, such as Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense), musk thistle (Carduus nutans) and bull thistle (Cirsium vulgare).  

The Colfax SWCD seeks funding to continue the effort of treating noxious weeds in the area. CSWCD has identified RME to implement the monitoring and treatments in the 450 acre project area. RME has a proven track record in the area, as they have assisted the NMSLO in monitoring and conducting treatments in the area. As such, they are intimately familiar with the general area which will assist with efficient project completion. RME will map AND treat thistles concurrently. The area will be treated with a team of up to 7 crew members equipped with backpack sprayers. Each team member will be familiar with local botany, and will utilize a mobile mapper to document thistle populations size and location. Following treatment, RME will return to the project area to map the area again, which will provide results for the monitoring. 

*Please note: this funding request is for a different treatment area than was previously applied and awarded for the FY25 NMDA grant program.

Herbicide treatments are highly cost effective and will yield a large treatment area as well as a high success rate in select thistle species, including Canada thistle which is prevalent in the project area. Additionally, residents within surrounding communities may see a decrease in wildfire potential with decreased understory fuel loading due to reduced populations of dense thistle.

column97: The noxious weeds identified for removal in this project spread aggressively in riparian landscapes and areas of disturbance such as burn scars. Most known infestations are in riparian areas, in the Whitewater Baldy burn scar, and likely in the Black Fire footprint. It is critical to put resources into treating infestations of target Class A, B, and C species before they spread throughout waterways and large disturbance areas. Providing funding for this effort will allow us to continue momentum from FY2025 treatments, increase efficacy of these treatments, and keep noxious weed infestations from becoming too large to feasibly manage. Maintaining the biodiversity of the Gila National Forest and Wilderness is a national, state, and local priority. Controlling invasive species in the upper watersheds of the river will help prevent movement of noxious weeds downstream into the farming communities of Gila and Cliff, NM, and support the outdoor recreation economy.
column98: The Gila River watershed is one of the most biodiverse networks of riparian areas in New Mexico that supports seven endangered species. Protecting the native riparian flora is critical to maintaining the habitat structure that supports these species.  It also provides one of the highest breeding bird concentrations in North America, including rare species such as the Gila Woodpecker and the threatened Southwestern Willow Flycatcher. Keeping this unique, biodiverse landscape intact aids in our efforts to combat climate change and stabilize New Mexico’s ecosystems. The characteristics of the Gila region contribute substantially to the regional tourist economy and maintaining wilderness character helps preserve the reasons people visit the area. This grant itself will generate new seasonal jobs that benefit young New Mexicans entering the work force. Controlling noxious weed infestations in headwaters areas will also prevent infestations downstream in agricultural areas, thereby avoiding potential economic impacts in agricultural communities.

column72: Sustainable Noxious Weed Management for Enhanced Agricultural Productivity
column73: Integrated Weed Management (On-the-Ground Treatments)
column77: This project focuses on controlling noxious weeds on agricultural land using either mechanical or chemical treatments. By collaborating with producers, we aim to reduce weed populations, improve land productivity, and provide sustainable land management solutions.
column78:
This project focuses on managing and controlling noxious weeds on agricultural land to improve land health and productivity. In collaboration with producers, we will implement either mechanical or chemical treatment methods, depending on the specific needs of the land and the extent of the weed infestation. This approach allows for flexibility while ensuring that effective weed control strategies are applied.

The first phase of the project will involve detailed surveying and mapping of the land to assess the spread and density of noxious weeds. Based on this data, we will determine the most appropriate treatment method. Mechanical treatments, such as mowing, tilling, or cutting, will be used to physically remove weeds and limit their ability to spread. Alternatively, chemical treatments will be used in areas where mechanical methods are less effective, applying herbicides in a targeted manner to minimize environmental impact while controlling stubborn weed populations.

Throughout the project, ongoing monitoring will ensure that treatments are effective and that any necessary follow-up actions are identified. The final phase will involve an evaluation of treatment success, including a comprehensive report on the reduction of noxious weeds and the overall improvement of land conditions. This project will provide producers with the tools and knowledge to manage noxious weeds sustainably, ensuring healthier land and more productive agricultural operations in the future.

The Central Curry Soil and Water Conservation District (SWCD) is enthusiastic about collaborating with local producers to address the issue of unwanted and noxious weeds in our region. Our expansive landscape, characterized by numerous acres of stunning rangeland, presents a unique opportunity for improvement. Our goal is to enhance the quality of this land for our producers by implementing effective brush control practices aimed at eliminating noxious weed species.
Through these efforts, we aim to foster the growth of beneficial native grasses, which will not only bolster the health of our ecosystems but also support the productivity of agricultural operations in the area. By working together, we can create a sustainable and thriving environment that benefits both our land and the producers who depend on it. We look forward to engaging with our community to ensure the success of these vital conservation initiatives.
column98:
The project aimed at controlling unwanted and noxious weeds in the area offers significant economic and environmental benefits for local residents. Economically, enhancing the quality of rangeland will increase agricultural productivity by promoting the growth of native grasses, which improves forage quality for livestock. This can lead to higher farm yields and increased property values, as healthy land is more desirable to potential buyers. Additionally, reducing the need for herbicides can result in cost savings for producers.
Environmentally, the project fosters biodiversity by restoring native plant communities, which supports a diverse range of wildlife. Improved soil health from native grasses enhances soil structure and fertility, reducing erosion and promoting better water retention. Furthermore, healthier rangelands contribute to water quality protection by minimizing runoff and sedimentation in local water bodies. Overall, this initiative enhances agricultural viability while promoting environmental stewardship and sustainability for the entire community.

Local agricultural organizations will offer insights into the specific challenges faced by producers, allowing us to tailor our approaches effectively. Conservation groups will contribute their knowledge in ecological restoration, strengthening our weed control efforts.
These partnerships will foster collaboration and community involvement. By leveraging the strengths of each partner, we can enhance the project's impact, ensuring sustainable outcomes that benefit both the environment and local agriculture, ultimately promoting healthier rangelands.

column72: Mechanical Removal and Follow Up Treatment for Russian Olives In Taos County
column73: Integrated Weed Management (On-the-Ground Treatments) Education and Outreach Surveying and Mapping
column77: This project will focus on mechanical removal of Russian Olive trees on Taos County private agricultural land and follow up treatments to address tree resprouting.
column78:
Taos SWCD will be working with private landowners in its district who seek assistance in removing Russian Olives and maintaining desirable vegetation in the treated areas.  The project's focus is particularly Russian Olives, but this species often presents along two other woody noxious weeds able to be controlled in a similar manner: Siberian Elm and Saltcedar.  Because of the scope of the problem, landowners will continue to apply for assistance and potential project sites will be evaluated by Taos SWCD staff to record acreage and density of infestation so as to get a specific sense of the scope of work involved to employ contractors in mechanically removing the Russian Olives.

Applicant parcels will be visited and mapped and ranked for suitability for district assistance in helping landowners remove the invasive species.  Taos SWCD will partner with contractors to mechanically remove Russian Olives and conduct managed goat grazing activities to deal with invasive species regrowth.  Alternatively, landowners will be provided technical assistance, equipment rental, and PPE for self-application of follow up herbicide treatments to deal with regrowth after initial treatment.   

For those who have already worked with Taos SWCD and had their property treated through mastication (scheduled for August 2025 with other funding) and cut stump treatment, there are opportunities in later 2025 for follow up treatment based on landowner preference and circumstance, whether that be a repeat herbicide basal bark treatment or a targeted goat grazing treatment.

column97: Over the last several decades since its introduction, Russian Olives have become established in riparian agricultural areas, taking over in riparian areas in which the noxious weeds are able to tap into shallow groundwater.   As Russian Olive populations have increased, native willows, cottonwoods, and other riparian species have been crowded out by the fast growing and quickly spreading noxious weed species.  Russian olives have continued to creep from stream channels further inward on subirrigated agricultural fields, where they interfere with historic and current land use practices involving domesticated livestock and forage production.  Many landowners have requested assistance from the Taos Soil and Water Conservation District to mitigate the spread of this species and reclaim pastures for agricultural use and improve the overall biodiversity of riparian areas.
column98:
Local landowners affected by Russian olive (and Siberian Elm and saltcedar) infestations would have improved opportunities for effectively maintaining the viability of their agricultural enterprises, not to mention improving the biodiversity of their landholdings, which has generally decreased as these invasive species have crowded out other desirable species.  

Fencelines and pastures would be easier to maintain and be more productive for traditional agricultural practices, such as haying and grazing beef cattle.  These land managers have specific equipment and knowledge around pursuing these practices, but generally do not have the required expertise or equipment (ie., correct herbicide selection, timing, and application techniques, not to mention heavy equipment suited toward eliminating heavy brush) to effectively manage the invasive species.
column99: Taos SWCD cooperated with Claunch-Pinto SWCD and the NM Water Trust Board to begin removing Russian Olives in 2025, treating 75 acres of infestations.
column100:
Based on project site requirements and best practices, Taos SWCD will work with contract herbicide applicators, contract heavy equipment operators, and contract livestock graziers to effectively remove targeted invasive species.  These partnerships are necessary for addressing the various stages of invasive species removal and maintenance, and they bring to bear a diversity of perspectives in managing the project as a whole.  The jury is still out regarding best practices for effective removal of the targeted species here in the specific context of Taos County.  

Approaching the removal and land maintenance process holistically, different potential partners (whether they are herbicide applicators, Americorps conservation crews doing chipping and mechanical removal, heavy equipment operators utilizing different machinery types, and goat graziers trained in undesirable woody vegetation management) provide different specialized viewpoints about what techniques are the most effective, given the constraints presented by each landowner's unique context.

column77:
The project proposes to do a variety of invasive species planning, prevention, and 
implementation activities on Santa Clara Pueblo lands in conjunction with our newly developed Santa Clara Pueblo 
Invasive Species Management Plan.
column78:
Santa Clara Pueblo has been invested in post fire restoration efforts while combating invasive species to return native plant communities.  Restoration efforts have made a difference in the control of non-native species: Russian olive, Saltcedar, and Siberian Elm.  These treated areas provide growing space for native cottonwoods and willow species.  However, resprouting continues and other non-native invasive plants are beginning to be a large-scale problem. Vegetation Surveys conducted in 2023 found 25 species of concern.  Six of the 25 species found during surveys are Class A listed species in New Mexico meaning that they are on the most wanted list, these include: Canada Thistle, Purple Loosestrife, Ravenna grass, Scotch Thistle, Spotted Knapweed, and Yellow Starthistle. Four Class B Species and seven Class C species were also detected during surveys along with six listed Troublesome Species and two species that were found to be concerning. Some of the species found, Eurasian watermilfoil, purple loosestrife, and 
whitewater crowfoot, are aquatic invasive species, which will likely require careful planning to successfully remove. 

The Invasive Plant Management Plan prioritizes treatments.  Priorities include eliminating eight localized invasive species outbreaks, treating areas along Santa Clara Creek and within Santa Clara Canyon, treating areas along the Rio Santa Cruz and the Rio Grande, and treating roadsides. Monitoring would be expanded, along with youth and community engagement. It is the hope of the Pueblos Invasive Management Plan that control efforts can reach positive successional vegetational change that will improve Santa Clara Pueblos natural resources health into the future.

column77: We propose integrating use of mowing and existing biological control agents (tamarisk leaf beetles) to reduce populations of tamarisk (saltcedar) at Caballo Reservoir. Green leaf volatiles (GLV) will be used to improve tamarisk leaf beetle efficacy.
column78:
Current management of tamarisk around Caballo New Mexico largely involves mechanical control in the form of mowing. While this reduces the tamarisk canopy temporarily, the trees resprout from the mowed stumps. Tamarisk must be mowed annually to prevent its spread and save water.

Tamarisk leaf beetles (Diorhabda spp.) are four species of approved biological control agents that have been present in New Mexico for nearly 15 years. Diorhabda can cause canopy dieback  but are less effective when large number of beetles are spread across a landscape, rather than concentrated on a single area. However, Diorhabda beetles are responsive to green leaf volatiles (GLV), which are produced naturally when Diorhabda feed on Tamarisk. The compounds that make up these GLV have been identified and can be synthesized. Lures containing GLV compounds are more potent than beetle feeding alone, and cause beetles to congregate on trees with lures, increasing herbivory on those targeted trees. Large numbers Diorhabda can defoliate trees, with repeated defoliation killing tamarisk trees. There is some evidence that late summer or fall defoliation is more detrimental to tamarisk trees than defoliation at other times of year. 

Combining biological control with other weed management techniques such as mowing can improve tamarisk control.  However, mowing can kill the Diorhabda beetles. GLV lures can be used to lure Diorhabda to select trees (i.e., refugia) which will not be mowed. This allows for a greater number of Diorhabda to survive, and these beetles will attack regrowth on mowed trees, increasing damage.

column97: Tamarisk grows densely along river banks or within reservoirs between the current water level and the high water mark. The plants use water that is designated for beneficial uses downstream. Thus, a goal of management is to remove existing tamarisk to save water. At Caballo Reservoir, as well as other reservoirs in New Mexico, tamarisk has established and has proven difficult to manage. Mowing of tamarisk and a biological control insect (tamarisk leaf beetle, Diorhabda spp.) both provide a means of tamarisk control, each with limited effectiveness. The combination of mowing and biocontrol provide a promising solution; however, little is known about how to implement mowing without damaging beetle populations. This project will test a blend of green leaf volatile compounds (GLVs) which can (1) be used to attract beetles to mature trees to improve control, and (2) aggregate beetles away from mowing operations to increase beetle survival.
column98: This project seeks to develop procedures to improve tamarisk management. These improvements will save water in the Rio Grande watershed and will save money on tamarisk management. At Caballo Reservoir alone, the Bureau of Reclamation mows approximately 4,000 acres annually at a cost of $40 per acre, for a total of $160,000 annually. Furthermore, these costs will only increase in the future, because the management strategy does not kill tamarisk, but rather only cuts back the current years' growth. Integrating mowing and the tamarisk leaf beetle could results in less mowing required and greater tamarisk mortality.

column77: Salt Cedar has infested riparian habitats and is spreading across our waterways, drainages and native grasslands. This initiative will build off previous salt cedar eradication efforts and include monitoring efforts and outreach with public/ stakeholders to collectively address the issue.
column78:
The focus of this project includes mechanical treatment in conjunction with chemical/ herbicide treatments. The target species for the bulk of this project is Salt Cedar. The most effective treatment for Salt Cedar at this point is cut-stump followed up with a basal/ remedy chemical treatment, which will be safe to use in riparian areas (aquatic friendly). Salt Cedar trees within the defined polygon (46 acres) , that are six (6) inches or more in diameter will be cut with chainsaws and the stumps will be treated with the herbicide mix. Any Salt Cedar less than six (6) inches in diameter will be treated with the specified chemical mixture. This method is very effective, especially in riparian areas, so that the larger trees are removed which will allow native species to re-establish, but the smaller species are killed, yet the skeletons will remain to help with wildlife habitat. Areas outside the defined polygon will be treated with the chemical mixure to help with the overall success of this project (8 acres +/-) approximately 55 acres total.
Other class A, B and C species are included within this project. African Rue, Russian Knapweed, Camelthorn, Purple starthistle, Scotch thistle, Bull Thistle, Malta starthistle, Perennial pepperweed, Spiny Cocklbur, and Russian Olive populations which have been treated with herbicides and mechanically, and will continue to be monitored and treated by CSWCD and assistance from partners and MOU's between other agencies and districts.  Monitoring before and after treatment will determine the effectiveness of the treatments.

column102:
The timeline for this project will begin July 15, 2025 thru October 31, 2026.:
After grant awards are finalized in July, the district will utilize the time between July and October to accurately map the defined treatment polygon with help from the contracted company Western Land Management and other partners. Collaboration on the accuracy of the polygon is crucial so that funding is spent to the best of its ability.

Mapping training will be requested from NMDA Noxious Weed Coordinator- Dylan Burrus, and contracted professional Clay Benton between July and October. Staff and other districts/ agencies could vastly benefit from mapping training particularly on Arc Pro and EddMapS. Both will be used to track the progress of this project and future projects as well as contribute to public available data on noxious weeds. 

During the cool fall and winter months October to February, the mechanical and chemical treatments will be implemented. These months are the most desired by the contractors, as the cooler weather will allow potentially dangerous snakes and other species to be in hibernation. Safety of staff and contractors is a top priority. This is also the timeline where beginning monitoring points will be established to track the success of the project once completed. 

Between March and June, post project monitoring will take place in the monitoring points as discussed above. 

During the entire duration of this project, Class A, B and C species will be mapped and logged into treatment categories based off priority locations and density of the species. Because Chaves SWCD and CWMA cover such a large landscape, this will be a collaborative effort between the district and partnering agencies. 

During the final quarter of this funding cycle, we will compile a start to finish presentation or document to advertise on our website as well as participate in the Eastern New Mexico State Fair with and educational booth for a duration of one week. At this time, our staff is in contact with thousands of public members, and we can share the challenges and successes of this project.

In this case, a producer could request cost share on chemical, with labor as their match to maintain treated areas, in conjunction with the districts efforts to retreat resprouts and whips. 
The district will also follow up the other Class A, B and C species and treat/ retreat those locations, and monitor the eradication progress. The long term goal in monitoring these projects will be to follow up annually and then semi-annually to ensure the areas are maintained.

column77: We will use funding to hire contractors for spraying, covering landowner costs for up to 100 acres, instead of employing one person. This approach maximizes efficiency and impact. Targeted noxious weeds are hoary cress, Russian knapweed, thistle, and others.
column78:
The district will utilize grant funding to contract with multiple independent contractors to develop and implement a noxious weeds program. Rather than hiring a single employee, the district will cover up to 100 acres of weed treatment per landowner by hiring contractors for spraying services. This method increases both efficiency and the program’s overall reach. Target species include hoary cress, Russian knapweed, thistle, African Rue, and other noxious weeds identified in the area. By working with independent contractors, the district avoids the added cost and delay of certifying new hires, allowing the program to launch immediately if funding is awarded. Contractors will not be employees of the Cuba SWCD and will be responsible for their own certifications, insurance, equipment, chemicals, and operations.
The program will begin with landowners submitting an application. Upon receipt, an assessor from the district will evaluate the property. Once approved, the landowner will receive a list of approved contractors to choose from. Each contractor will provide a project estimate, and the landowner will be required to pay their 25% cost share upfront before work begins. The grant will cover the remaining 75% of the project cost. To ensure completion and accountability, the district will require before-and-after photos of each project site. The program will continue until either the funding is exhausted..

column97: Noxious weeds pose a serious threat to agricultural productivity, native plant biodiversity, and overall land health within our district. These invasive species—such as hoary cress, Russian knapweed, and various thistles—outcompete native vegetation, degrade soil quality, reduce forage availability for livestock and wildlife, and increase long-term land management costs for producers and landowners. Many of our constituents lack the equipment, knowledge, or resources to effectively control these invasive weeds on their own.
column98: This project aims to provide timely, cost-effective weed management by contracting qualified professionals to carry out targeted herbicide applications. By offering landowners financial support and access to skilled contractors, the district will improve treatment success, encourage proactive land stewardship, and prevent further spread of noxious weeds. Utilizing independent contractors eliminates the need for costly and time-consuming staff certifications and allows the program to launch quickly upon funding approval. Additionally, requiring landowner cost-share ensures commitment and sustainability while maximizing the reach of available funds. This collaborative, results-driven approach supports both environmental health and agricultural resilience across the district.

column78:
Roadrunner Public Health will implement a comprehensive noxious weed and vegetation management program for the City of Belen, targeting both winter and summer weed growth on City-owned properties and rights-of-way. This public health initiative includes pre-emergent and post-emergent herbicide treatments to control invasive and noxious weed species throughout the year. By clearing overgrown vegetation, the program aims to reduce mosquito breeding grounds, mitigate fire risk, and improve the overall appearance and safety of public spaces.

In addition to protecting public health by limiting potential mosquito-borne illnesses, the vegetation management effort will enhance community well-being and support environmental stewardship. The City will prioritize high-traffic areas, drainage channels, and other sites with high vegetation density or public health concerns. Regular monitoring and follow-up treatments will ensure effectiveness and sustainability. This initiative reflects the City’s commitment to maintaining clean, safe, and healthy public environments for all residents and visitors.

The City will cut down noxious weeds after the summer growing season and then Roadrunner Public Health will use EsplAnade 200 SC and Ranger Pro products or similar for Pre and Post Emergent noxious weed management applications in the fall of 2025. Breakthrough growth will be treated in the summer. This program is our first for noxious weed management; however, the City is committed to carrying it our past the grant performance period and have budgeted for ongoing treatments as needed after this first year.

column97:
The City of Belen faces ongoing challenges with noxious weed overgrowth on public property and rights-of-way, particularly during peak growing seasons. These overgrown areas not only create visual blight but also pose significant public health and safety risks. Dense weed growth provides ideal conditions for mosquito breeding, increasing the potential for the spread of mosquito-borne diseases such as West Nile Virus. Additionally, unmanaged vegetation contributes to fire hazards, obstructs sidewalks and roadways, and can damage infrastructure.

Without regular and effective vegetation control, the City struggles to maintain safe, accessible, and healthy public spaces. Current municipal resources are insufficient to address the widespread and seasonal nature of the issue, resulting in inconsistent treatment and long-term regrowth. This project is necessary to establish a proactive and systematic approach to noxious weed management, reduce public health threats, and improve the livability of our community.
column98:
This project will provide economic and environmental benefits for residents by improving public health, reducing maintenance costs, and protecting local ecosystems. Environmentally, targeted vegetation management will control the spread of invasive and noxious weed species that threaten native plants and disrupt natural habitats. Reducing mosquito harborage will also help minimize the use of chemical treatments and prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses.

Economically, the project will reduce the need for emergency weed abatement and reactive mosquito control measures, resulting in cost savings. Clean, well-maintained public spaces can also boost property values and encourage economic activity by improving the overall appearance and safety of the community. Additionally, proactive weed control helps protect public infrastructure—such as sidewalks, drainage systems, and roadways—from damage caused by unchecked vegetation growth, avoiding costly repairs over time.

By investing in preventative maintenance, the City creates a more attractive, sustainable, and economically resilient environment for its residents.

We own a 20 acre public park in Taos, adjacent to a 20 acre Taos municipal open space. We are parciantes on the Vigil y Romo Acequia, which includes the Town of Taos and property owners of 5 additional acres in the project area. 

We've mapped and addressed Class A, Class B, and Class C species within the project area. For each species of concern, we laid out two 30m X 30m plots with 3m X 3m subplots to monitor pre-and-post treatment inventory. We will continue to treat and inventory with a seasonal youth conservation corps crew as part of our long term ecological monitoring program. Phase 2 treatment methods include physical, mechanical, cultural with contracted goat grazing, fire with individual blow torch applications, and chemical with high strength vinegar application. In Phase 2 we seek equipment such as a rotary cutter and a portable sawmill to scale up our treatments. We also plan to rent this equipment to community to support treatment efforts in the Taos area. 

We will host additional public workshops to share our results. We will continue to mill suitable material for use on the property. We have built two park benches with Russian olive and received a $21,000 grant to purchase tools to create a wood shop to expand our capacity to repurpose materials. Work will take place between July 2025 and June 2026. Partners include the Town of Taos, Taos Land Trust, and the Vigil y Romo Acequia.

column77: Ancestral Lands Conservation Corps will partner with the Pueblo of Sandia to address critical conservation needs along the Bosque, treating priority invasive woody species that have severe negative impacts on the health of the Rio Grande and its surrounding forest.
column78:
Ancestral Lands Conservation Corps (ALCC), a program of Conservation Legacy, engages Indigenous youth in conservation projects that reconnect them to the land, mentorship, and economic opportunity. The proposed project will recruit youth in restoring the Rio Grande’s Bosque in the Pueblo of Sandia that is endangered by Class C noxious weeds including Siberian elm, Russian olive, saltcedar, and tree of heaven. Each species drastically affects the ecology of the Bosque by sapping water resources, providing excessive wildfire fuel, and outcompeting native species. The project area was treated over 10 years ago. The goal is to retreat and eradicate new and resprouts of non-native trees. 

ALCC will recruit a crew of six youth to restore 37 acres. Youth will gain industry-recognized certifications and skills including herbicide application, tool safety and handling, chainsaw operations, and Wilderness First Aid. The crew's treatments will begin in August and follow the treatment plan for the area. The project will meet immediate needs while increasing the future land management capacity of the Pueblo and other agencies by training the next generation of land managers.  

On-the-ground treatment methods for tree of heaven will be spray only - trees up to chest height will be foliar sprayed and larger trees will receive the hack & squirt method. All other species will be cut & sprayed. Smaller trees will be chipped and larger trees will be hauled off-site to be utilized as biochar as soil amendment in the Pueblo. The herbicide will be triclopyr (Garlon 4 or equivalent).

Sediment from upstream dams and these invasive species have pushed the Bosque into a monospecific stand with a homogenous canopy, making the forest more at risk of disease and catastrophic fire. In addition to the depth of conservation needs, the Pueblo has limited capacity to address them. column100: Ancestral Lands Conservation Corps has a positive working relationship with the Pueblo of Sandia which has led to the design of this project that will help the Pueblo meet critical conservation goals while providing youth with impactful learning and service opportunities. While the Pueblo has a Bosque Program with a crew to manage the Bosque, partnerships like those formed with ALCC are necessary in helping to manage the over 800 acres that are in the program’s care. Due to high propagation and how widespread Class C noxious weeds are, regular treatment is required to maintain a healthy forest and watershed. This project will continue the efforts to restore the health and resilience of the Bosque and retreat an area that was first treated over 10 years ago to eradicate new and resprouted non-native trees.
